statements.quote: Modern AI is, at its core, applied linear algebra.
Every image, every word, every token lives in a high-dimensional **vector space**.
This chapter introduces the mathematical objects that make neural networks possible: vectors, matrices, tensors, and the operations that combine them.
If you complete this chapter, the rest of the textbook, embeddings, attention, gradients, activations, will read as natural applications of these primitives.
In 1D, you only have one “degree of freedom.” You can go forward or backward.
* **Concept:** A single number describes your entire universe.
By adding a second number, we unlock an infinite flat surface.
\citealternativetitle{rgb_color_cube}: every color in this RGB color cube is a single point inside it, located by its Red, Green, and Blue coordinates.
We cannot “see” 4D, but we can **describe** it.
In AI, dimensions are just “features.” Imagine we are describing a “Fruit.” We can use a 4D vector to describe:
Every fruit is now a point in a 4D “Fruit Space.”

The geometric picture above is intuitive, but it hides a question: when we add a vector to a vector, or stretch a vector by a number, *what rules must those operations obey?* A **vector space** is the precise answer.
Mathematicians formalize this as follows.
Pick a *base field* $k$ — a number system where addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division all behave as you would expect.
In this course, $k$ will almost always be the **real numbers** $\mathbb{R}$; in cryptography or some physics contexts it might be a finite field or the complex numbers.

A *vector space over $k$* is a set $V$ together with two operations — vector addition $V \times V \to V$ and scalar multiplication $k \times V \to V$ — that satisfy eight axioms (closure, associativity, identity, inverses, distributivity, compatibility of scalar multiplication), as \cite[Axler lists them in Linear Algebra Done Right (Ch.
12)]{axler2024linearalgebra}.
The elements of $V$ are called **vectors**; the elements of $k$ are called **scalars**.
A **scalar** is a single number from the base field — in this course, almost always a real number.
You use scalars every time you stretch a vector or measure a single quantity.
A note on terminology: in machine learning, you will often see "scalar" used more loosely to mean "a single number of any kind" — for example a pixel brightness in $\{0, 1, \ldots, 255\}$.
That is fine as a casual usage, but strictly speaking that *set* is not a field (no negatives, no quotients), so it cannot be the base field $k$ of a vector space.

The values are *discrete integers* (a subset of $\mathbb{Z}$), not real numbers in the strict mathematical sense; storing them as floats or treating them as elements of $\mathbb{R}$ is a computational convention that lets you run arithmetic on them, not a statement about what kind of object they are.
The two meanings rarely cause problems in practice; just be aware they exist.
A **vector** is an element of a vector space.

The geometric picture is an *arrow* with a direction and a length: "three steps to the right, four steps up." The algebraic picture is a single thing you can add to other vectors and stretch with scalars.
If you pick a basis, you can write a vector as a list of coordinates.
In $\mathbb{R}^3$ with the standard basis (\cite[Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right, §2B, p.
39]{axler2024linearalgebra}), the arrow "3 right, 4 up, 2 forward" becomes the column
Two important properties:
* A vector is *not glued to one spot*.
The arrow "3 right, 4 up" is the same arrow whether you draw it starting at the origin or at $(1, 1)$.
This is what it means for vectors to be *free* (not anchored to a point).
* You can stretch a vector by a scalar: $2 \cdot (3, 4, 2) = (6, 8, 4)$.
You can add vectors component-wise: $(1, 2) + (3, 4) = (4, 6)$.
To make a color, a computer needs a list of 3 numbers: one for Red, one for Green, one for Blue.
This 3-tuple is a vector in $\mathbb{R}^3$:
Two independent births stand behind that picture.

In 1843 William Rowan Hamilton found the rule $i^2=j^2=k^2=ijk=-1$ and reported it to the Royal Irish Academy that November; the four-part objects he called *quaternions* multiplied non-commutatively, so $ab \neq ba$ (\cite[Hamilton, 1844]{hamilton1844quaternions}).

A year later Hermann Grassmann's *Ausdehnungslehre* built a coordinate-free algebra of $n$-dimensional extensions, complete with subspaces, bases and exterior products (\cite[Grassmann, 1844]{grassmann1844ausdehnungslehre}).
Hamilton's vectors lived inside a 4-D algebra; Grassmann's lived in a space of any dimension.
Modern linear algebra inherits from both.
A vector is *not glued to one spot*.
The arrow "3 right, 4 up" is the same arrow whether you draw it starting at the origin or somewhere else.
Vectors can have any number of dimensions.
Two essential operations on vectors:
**Scalar multiplication** multiplies each coordinate:
Vectors can also be added:
A **Matrix** is a grid of numbers (like a spreadsheet).
A **Black & White photo** is just a Matrix.
Each spot in the grid tells the computer how bright that specific pixel is, when we say $0$ means “black”, $255$ means white and everything inbetween are different shades of gray.

Historically, a matrix began as a *bookkeeping device*: Sylvester's oblong array existed so that one could pick square sub-arrays and form determinants from them (\cite[Sylvester, 1850]{sylvester1850matrix}).
Cayley's 1858 memoir changed its status.

He defined addition, multiplication and inversion of matrices, checked that a $2\times2$ matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation, and introduced the "transposed matrix" (\cite[Cayley, 1858]{cayleymemoirmatrices}).
A grid of numbers became an object with an algebra — the step that lets a neural network's weight matrix be multiplied, inverted and differentiated.
You have seen scalars, vectors, and matrices.

statements.quote: So far a tensor was just *data* — numbers arranged in a shape.
But you can also *compute* with it, and two operations power almost everything that follows.
**Element-wise.** Combine the matching entries of two tensors, one by one.
The tensors do not even need the same shape: shapes are lined up from the right, an axis of length $1$ stretches to match, and a missing leading axis counts as $1$.
This rule is called **broadcasting** \cite[Broadcasting, NumPy]{numpy_broadcasting} — and it quietly explains the $\mathbf{x}+b$ of every affine layer.
**Contraction.** Multiply entries along a shared axis and add them up.

The matrix product is exactly one contraction, $M_{ik}=\sum_{j} \underbrace{C_{ij}}_{\text{row of C}}\,\underbrace{D_{jk}}_{\text{column of D}}$, where the index $j$ that appears twice is summed over and then hidden — the *summation convention* Einstein introduced in 1916 (\cite[Einstein, 1916]{einstein1916annalen}).
Contraction is the single most important operation in both linear algebra and deep learning.
Each word is old, and each was coined to solve a concrete problem.
- **Matrix** — from Latin *mātrix*, "womb or mold," ultimately *māter*, "mother" \cite[matrix, Etymonline]{etymonline_matrix}.

Sylvester's problem was bookkeeping: building the invariant theory of eliminants, he needed a way to line up a determinant's terms so he could juggle them, and in 1850 he called the result a *matrix* — "a Matrix out of which we may form various systems of determinants" (\cite[Sylvester, 1850]{sylvester1850matrix}).

Cayley's problem was different: he wanted linear transformations to behave like numbers you can multiply and compose, and his 1858 "arithmetic of matrices" gave them exactly that (\cite[Cayley, 1858]{cayleymemoirmatrices}).
- **Determinant** — the object the matrix was invented to organise is older than the matrix itself.

Seki Takakazu computed determinants in Japan by 1683, and Leibniz sent determinant-like "resultants" to l'Hôpital in a letter of 1693 (\cite[MacTutor: Matrices and determinants]{mactutor_matrices_determinants}).

Gabriel Cramer stated the general rule for solving $n$ linear equations with determinants in 1750, without proof (\cite[Cramer, 1750]{cramer1750introduction}); Cauchy gave the word its modern sense only in 1812.
- **Vector** — from Latin *vĕctōr*, "a carrier," from *vĕhĕre*, "to carry" \cite[vector, Etymonline]{etymonline_vector}.

Hamilton wanted to do 3-D geometry the way complex numbers do 2-D: a "calculus of direction" that adds and rotates directed line segments in space without writing out every component (\cite[Hamilton, 1854]{hamiltonextensionsquaternions}).
- **Scalar** — from Latin *scalaris*, "of a ladder" (*scala*, a single step) \cite[scalar, Etymonline]{etymonline_scalar}.

It is Hamilton's word for the direction-free *amount* of a quantity — the part you can add and multiply like an ordinary number, split off from the direction a *vector* carries (\cite[Hamilton, 1854]{hamiltonextensionsquaternions}).
- **A note on the dates** — Hamilton pairs *scalar* and *vector* explicitly in his 1846 *Philosophical Magazine* paper: "the algebraically real part ...
the scalar" and the imaginary part "may be called the vector part" (\cite[Hamilton, 1846]{hamilton1846quaternions}).
The word *vector* itself is older — astronomers spoke of a *radius vector* — but Hamilton gave it the algebraic sense used here (\cite[Miller: vector]{miller_vector}).
- **Tensor** — the English word dates to 1704, a Modern Latin agent noun from *tendere*, "to stretch" \cite[tensor, Etymonline]{etymonline_tensor}.
Hamilton gave it a mathematical life, using it for the length of a quaternion.

The modern object had to solve Voigt's problem: a crystal's properties depend on the direction you probe them (stiffness, light, heat flow), and he needed one object to hold all those directional couplings — his "Tensoren," 1898 (\cite[Voigt, 1898]{voigt1898krystalle}).

Ricci-Curbastro and Levi-Civita then built the calculus that makes tensors work, 1900, so that the laws of geometry could be written with no privileged coordinate system — the language Einstein inherited for relativity (\cite[Ricci-Curbastro & Levi-Civita, 1900]{riccilevicivita1900}; \cite[Einstein, 1916]{einstein1916annalen}).

- **Summation convention** — Einstein's 1916 answer to the tedium of long sums in his new tensor equations: an index that appears twice is summed over and then vanishes from the page (\cite[Einstein, 1916]{einstein1916annalen}).
Two details sharpen that story.

Voigt's word is not a definition of the modern tensor: he writes that he will call "die für sie charakteristischen physikalischen Grössen aber Tensoren" — the physical quantities characteristic of anisotropic crystals, "tensors" (\cite[Voigt, 1898]{voigt1898krystalle}).

And Ricci-Curbastro and Levi-Civita's 1900 memoir does not use the noun at all; it speaks of *systèmes* with covariant and contravariant components (\cite[Ricci-Curbastro & Levi-Civita, 1900]{riccilevicivita1900}; \cite[Miller: tensor]{miller_tensor}).
The noun travelled from Voigt's crystallography into Einstein's relativity; the calculus came from the Italians.

> **One idea, many names.** Determinants came first (Seki 1683, Leibniz 1693), matrices were named for bookkeeping (Sylvester 1850), matrix algebra arrived in 1858 (Cayley), and tensors travelled from quaternions (Hamilton 1846) through crystallography (Voigt 1898) into relativity (Einstein 1916).
The array is the modern container; the history is the set of problems it was built to hold.
In programming and math, we often want to take the result of one function and plug it directly into another.
This is called **composition**.
If we have a function $f$ and a function $g$, applying $f$ first and then $g$ is written as $(g \circ f)(x)$, which is just a shorthand for $g(f(x))$.

A deep network is built exactly this way: each layer is a function acting on the previous layer's output, so the whole network is a **chain of composed functions**, and — in Olah's framing — the role that *types* play in programming is played by *representations*: two layers can be composed only when the output representation of one matches the input the next expects (\cite[Olah, 2015]{colah2015types}).
The word *function* is older than the notation.

Leibniz used it in a 1673 manuscript for a line that "performs some function" in a figure; Johann Bernoulli described it in 1694 as "a quantity somehow formed from indeterminate and constant quantities" (\cite[MacTutor: The Function Concept]{macTutorFunctions}).
Euler introduced the symbol $f(x)$ in 1734 and made the function the central object of analysis in his 1748 *Introductio* (\cite[Miller: Function Symbols]{miller_functionsymbols}).
Once a function has a name, composition is just substitution: write $g(\;)$ and put $f(x)$ inside.
You can experiment with how two linear functions combine.
Adjust the sliders to see how the “inner” function $f$ and the “outer” function $g$ create a new, composed result.
We can visualize these relationships using a triangle diagram.
It shows that there are two ways to reach the same result: either you transform your data first and then apply a function, or you apply a modified version of that function to your raw data.

In Category Theory, $A, B, C$ are *objects* (which can be any mathematical objects, like sets) and $f$ and $g$ (the arrows) are so-called *morphisms* (which can be anything that connects mathematical objects to each other, like functions).
When both paths lead to the same result, we say the diagram **commutes**.

The **Hadamard Product** ($\odot$) was introduced by \citeauthor{hadamardproduct} to study **singularities** in complex power series: the term-by-term product and the related **Hadamard multiplication theorem** belong to his 1899 *Acta Mathematica* paper \citetitle{hadamard1899series}.

It is defined for vectors as $\vec{a} \odot \vec{b} = (a_1 b_1, \dots, a_n b_n)^T$ — the coefficients are multiplied term by term — which is exactly what lets one predict the analytic continuation and boundaries of functions derived from known ones.
The history is a little more tangled than the name suggests.

Hadamard's 1892 thesis was about Taylor series and analytic continuation; the term-by-term product and its multiplication theorem belong to his 1899 *Acta Mathematica* paper (\cite[Hadamard, 1899]{hadamard1899series}).

For matrices the key result is Schur's: the Hadamard product of two positive-semidefinite matrices is positive-semidefinite, proved as Theorem VII of his 1911 paper (\cite[Schur, 1911]{schur1911bilinear}).
The name "Hadamard product" for the matrix operation was popularised by Paul Halmos, who recalled that John von Neumann suggested it (\cite[Hadamard product, Wikipedia]{hadamard_product_wiki}).
While standard matrix multiplication follows the “row-by-column” rule, the **Hadamard Product** (also known as the *element-wise product*) is much more straightforward.
It takes two matrices or vectors of the **same dimensions** and multiplies the elements that occupy the same position.
In the context of Deep Learning, the $\odot$ symbol is ubiquitous.

It is used in **Layer Normalization** to scale normalized values by a learnable parameter $\gamma$, and in **Gating Mechanisms** (like LSTMs or GRUs) to decide which information should pass through a “gate.”

Transposing a matrix means flipping it over its main diagonal, turning rows into columns and columns into rows.
If $A$ is an $m \times n$ matrix with elements $a_{ij}$, then the transpose $A^T$ is an $n \times m$ matrix where $(A^T)_{ij} = A_{ji}$ (\cite[Boyd & Vandenberghe, Applied Linear Algebra, §6.3.1, p.
115]{boyd2018appliedlinearalgebra}).
The idea of matrix transposition was introduced in 1858 by the British mathematician \citeauthor{cayleymemoirmatrices} in his paper \citetitle{cayleymemoirmatrices}.
It arose from the study of bilinear and quadratic forms, where swapping rows and columns was needed to express symmetry properties.
Cayley's own wording is precise: "A matrix compounded with the transposed matrix gives rise to a symmetrical matrix" (\cite[Cayley, 1858]{cayleymemoirmatrices}).
The operation was thus born with matrix algebra, not added later: $A^T A$ and $AA^T$ are the symmetric Gram matrices of the rows and columns of $A$.
Cayley wrote the operation out in words; the modern superscript notation is later.
Two vector operations appear so often in AI that they deserve explicit definitions here, even though they are first motivated in the Statistics and Loss chapters.
Given a vector of real-valued scores $\vec{z} \in \mathbb{R}^{K}$ (called **logits**), the **softmax** turns it into a vector of probabilities that sum to $1$:
The exponential emphasises differences: a logit gap of $1$ becomes a ratio of $e \approx 2.7$, a gap of $2$ becomes $e^2 \approx 7.4$.
This is the operation behind the output layer of a classification network and behind every next-token probability in an LLM (see the Attention chapter).
The formula is older than machine learning.

It is the **Boltzmann distribution** of statistical mechanics — Boltzmann's 1868 paper, Gibbs's textbook of 1902 — with the logits playing the role of negative energies (\cite[Boltzmann distribution]{boltzmann_distribution_wiki}).
Duncan Luce derived it from his choice axiom in 1959 (\cite[Luce, 1959]{luce1959individualchoice}).
The name "softmax" is John Bridle's; he used it for a normalised exponential in a 1989 conference paper published in 1990 (\cite[Bridle, 1990]{bridle1990softmax}).
